how_it_wins:
Here is the first thing to get right: Yawgmoth is a draw engine wearing a kill's reputation. "Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card" costs no mana at all. The price is life and bodies, and you pay it at instant speed, on any turn, under any tax. He is on the battlefield by turn six in 91.3% of goldfish games, mean turn 4.287, and 7,208 of 10,000 runs cast him exactly on four.

Now the number that organises your whole game. By turn 10 this deck assembles one of its two kills in 4.6% of games on its own draws, and in 31.4% once the five tutors are allowed to fetch the missing half. Read those together and never apart: 4.6% is a floor that excludes tutors, rituals and cost reducers, and 31.4% is the estimate. That 27-point gap is what Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Beseech the Mirror, Diabolic Intent and Insatiable Avarice actually buy you, and it is the largest single contribution any five slots make.

So two games in three have no kill, and every game has an engine. Pace for the engine. By turn 10 renewable fodder is in hand 78.6% of the time unassisted and 92.3% tutor-assisted, a free sacrifice outlet 78.0% / 92.1%, an ignition source 73.5% / 90.6%, and a drain 60.8% / 85.4%. Those are a control deck's opening figures in every column, and Yawgmoth converts every one of them into cards nobody can Counterspell.

Then the honest part, because it changes how you aim. Three separate verified stacks measured a fully assembled engine at seven drains — 28 life across a four-player pod, taking the table from 40 to 33. That is a clock, not a kill. Stacks 002, 003 and 005 all land on the same figure by different routes and all end the same way: body exhaustion, not life, not library.

Which means you do not go for the pod. You go for a seat. Count spare bodies before the first activation, add the toughness your board can absorb above 1, and check that number against the lowest life total at the table. An opponent's untapped board is fuel — a 2/2 they control extends the engine by two activations (stack 002) — so the worst board this deck can face is an empty one. Take one player out, keep the cards the attempt drew, and do it again next turn.

combo_lines.001: The court begins with an intervening "if," and it is the whole case: "Whenever a creature dies, if it had a -1/-1 counter on it, put a -1/-1 counter on target creature." That condition is checked twice — once when the trigger would go on the stack and again on resolution — and the Insect Blowfly Infestation just targeted is still wearing the counter when it dies. So the loop is genuinely unbounded, and stack 001 says so. Now the holding nobody expects: on a bare board it is also drainless. State-based actions kill the counter-bearing token before Nest of Scarabs' trigger resolves, so when Blowfly's mandatory "target creature" needs a target, the only creature left is your drain — which therefore dies on iteration one, for a grand total of 3 life per opponent. The deficiency is exactly one body. Start the loop with your drain plus two other creatures and 38 completed iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0. And no, the mandatory loop is not a draw under CR 104.4b: you may order Blowfly's trigger above the Nest's, empty the battlefield of creatures, and leave the next trigger with no legal target.
combo_lines.002: Relish the clause that bounds everything: "up to one target creature." Yawgmoth is a 2/4 and could happily absorb four counters, except that protection from Humans makes him untargetable by his own ability (CR 702.16b, 113.7) — and he is a Human Cleric. So every counter has to land somewhere else, and once the opponent's body is gone the only legal targets are your own 1/1 tokens. The plain-English holding: bodies bound this engine, and the number is seven. Five completed activations, seven of your creatures die, Bastion of Remembrance triggers seven times, each opponent goes 40 to 33 — 28 life removed from a pod of 160. The checker did not take that on trust; it derived the bound algebraically and proved seven is a ceiling, not merely the line taken. Bastion earns its place by being an enchantment: it is never fodder and never a target, which is why this board banks its last drain. Spend {B}{B} and a card on Yawgmoth's proliferate and the figure is 8 drains and 32 life — a property of that line, not of the board.
combo_lines.003: The elegant part is a rule about time. CR 603.6c and 603.10a make a leaves-the-battlefield trigger look back at the game as it was just before the event, so Zulaport Cutthroat's own death still sees Zulaport on the battlefield and pays out. Add CR 115.6, which lets "up to one target" mean zero targets, and CR 601.2h, which lets you choose the sacrifice — and the holding follows cleanly: you are never forced to eat your own drain. Zulaport survives every iteration and is spent deliberately, last, where its death banks the seventh drain. Seven drains, 28 life, each opponent 40 to 33. It caps at seven precisely because Zulaport is itself a body that must eventually die. Note the figure matches stack 002 exactly and note why that means nothing: two different boards, two different limiting mechanisms, one coincidence of arithmetic. It is not corroboration.
combo_lines.004: One word decides this case, and it is "target." Blood Artist reads "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life" — a single player per trigger, chosen one at a time. Against three opponents on 40 apiece that is a rounding error, and the checker says so in as many words: NOT A KILL, AND NOT EVEN CLOSE. The board's number is eight. Eight creature deaths, eight triggers, eight life removed from a pod of 160, with an exhaustive search of the line space finding nothing better. Set that beside stack 003's 28 from the same shape of board and you have the exchange rate printed: single-target reach costs a factor of 3.5 against "each opponent loses 1 life." There is a small indignity at the end, too. Yawgmoth's protection bars him as a target and "another creature" bars him as the sacrifice, so the last legal target is Blood Artist itself — the engine finishes by eating its own payoff.
combo_lines.005: Savour CR 119.9, because it is the sharpest fact in the deck: gaining 0 life is not a life gain event. South Wind Avatar reads "Whenever another creature you control dies, you gain life equal to its toughness" and then "Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life." So an Insect you sacrifice to Yawgmoth dies at last known toughness 1, gains you 1, and drains the table. An Insect killed by its own -1/-1 counter dies at toughness 0, gains you nothing, and the drain never fires at all. Eight death triggers, seven nonzero gains, seven drains — 28 opposing life, each opponent 40 to 33, ended by body exhaustion at eight completed activations. The Avatar's other job is measured just as exactly: its 4 toughness is worth +4 activations and supplies all of the damage. The checker proved the ceiling by exhausting every way the Avatar can leave the battlefield, and ruled out proliferate as a way past it. Commander Spellbook's "Near-infinite" tag on this pairing is refuted for this board.
combo_lines.006: Here is a rule most pilots have never read and every -1/-1 deck should know by heart. CR 122.6 says a reference to counters being put on an object covers an object that is given counters as it enters the battlefield — not only counters placed on something already there. Persist returns a creature "with a -1/-1 counter on it" and names no player, so CR 122.6a assigns the counter to the object's controller, which is you. The holding: Nest of Scarabs triggers, and you get an Insect. Note the route, because it matters. This does not run through CR 608.2c, the rule the other five stacks lean on — 608.2c names the spell's controller and 122.6a names the object's, and they diverge the moment a permanent enters under an opponent's control. Then the practical catch. Persist on Fume Spitter returns a 1/1 that enters as a 0/0 and is dead to state-based actions before the trigger even resolves. You keep the Insect, not the body — so aim it at something whose toughness survives the ride.

card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: The engine, and he is a draw engine before he is a kill: "Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card" costs no mana at all, so taxes and Winter Orb effects never touch it. Protection from Humans cuts both ways — it blanks a slice of the format's removal and it makes him untargetable by his own ability, which is what bounds every verified stack.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: The hub. "Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create that many 1/1 black Insect creature tokens" replaces the body each activation spends — but only one, and only after the death, so the loop is body-neutral only while the counter lands on something that lives. Note the retrieval graph has no entry for it at all; the deck's most important card is invisible to the synergy shortlist.
card_roles.Blowfly Infestation: Free, repeatable ignition and half of the deck's headline kill: every creature that dies wearing a -1/-1 counter puts another one somewhere. Stack 001 verified the loop as unbounded and also proved it drainless on a bare board — bring your drain plus two spare bodies and 38 iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: The best drain in the 99 for the simplest reason: it is an enchantment, so it is never fodder and never a target. Stack 002 measured a full engine at seven Bastion triggers, 28 life across the pod, and it banked the last one because nothing could eat it.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: Each-opponent drain on a 1/1 body, worth 28 opposing life on a full engine (stack 003). It caps at seven drains precisely because it is a creature that must eventually die — though CR 603.6c means its own death still pays, so spend it deliberately and spend it last.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Reach and a removal partner, not a payoff you assemble toward. "Target player loses 1 life" is single-target, and stack 004 priced that at 8 life from a 160-life pod — a factor of 3.5 behind Zulaport. It still triggers on any creature dying anywhere, which is why every removal spell in the deck carries a Removal + Death Trigger edge to it.
card_roles.South Wind Avatar: Two jobs in one 3/4 body: an each-opponent drain routed through lifegain, and the deck's best counter sink. Stack 005 priced the toughness at exactly +4 activations — and found the carve-out, since an Insect killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0 and CR 119.9 says gaining 0 is no gain at all.
card_roles.Mirkwood Bats: The only payoff in the 99 that reads token creation rather than death — "Whenever you create or sacrifice a token, each opponent loses 1 life" — which is exactly the half of Nest of Scarabs' output that nothing else monetises. Two readings are queued for the checker and neither is fact: whether it collects twice per Yawgmoth activation, and what it pays on the Blowfly loop, which sacrifices nothing.
card_roles.Ophiomancer: "At the beginning of each upkeep" — each, not yours — so at a four-player table this is up to four free deathtouch Snakes per turn cycle if you spend each one before the next upkeep. Read the condition before you deploy it: it makes nothing while you control a Snake, and South Wind Avatar is a Snake.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: A free body every upkeep for 1 life, and the single best turn-two play in the deck. Faerie Rogues are fodder, chump blockers and Skullclamp targets, and it rebuilds through a sweeper without any help.
card_roles.Grave Titan: Six power of deathtouch that brings two 2/2 Zombies on arrival and two more on every attack — bodies with toughness 2, which in this deck means counter sinks that pay an extra activation each.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: Undying for every non-Human you control, which is most of the board — and pointedly not Yawgmoth, who is a Human Cleric. He headlines eight of the deck's two-card infinites and half its bracket floor; not one of those lines has been verified, so play him as a resilience engine and treat the rest as a projection.
card_roles.Carnifex Demon: A 6/6 flier that arrives with two -1/-1 counters and turns each of them into a board-wide sweep of counters for {B}. Two activations of repeatable ignition on a body big enough to survive its own work.
card_roles.Massacre Girl, Known Killer: Menace on a 4/4, wither on your whole team, and a draw every time an opponent's creature dies with toughness below 1. She carries the deck's highest-scoring synergy edge to Yawgmoth — sacrifice, death trigger, draw-and-discard and -1/-1 all at once.
card_roles.Skinrender: Three -1/-1 counters on a single target when it enters, which is three Insects off Nest of Scarabs in one event and a dead creature on most boards. The cleanest single ignition in the deck.
card_roles.Soul Snuffers: A counter on every creature, yours included — a one-sided sweeper against a token board and mass ignition on your own. Note it hits each creature separately, and how the Nest counts a spread like that has not been settled by a stack.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: One mana of ignition you can hold up: sacrifice it, place a counter, start the chain. Stack 006 names the trap — reanimated with Persist it enters as a 0/0 and dies to state-based actions, so you keep the Insect and not the body.
card_roles.Necropede: A two-mana artifact creature that places a counter when it dies, so it is fodder and ignition in one slot. Infect means its combat damage lands as -1/-1 counters too, which the Nest reads as counters you put.
card_roles.Sinister Gnarlbark: A 0/4 that draws you a card and blights 1 at every end step — free, repeatable ignition on a body whose toughness soaks three counters before it dies. Quietly one of the best-shaped cards in the list.
card_roles.Necroskitter: Wither on a 1/4, and the payoff clause is theft: any creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter comes back under your control. Every ignition spell in the deck doubles as a reanimation trigger while it is out.
card_roles.Retched Wretch: A 4/2 that soaks a counter, lives at 3/1, and on its oracle text returns when it dies carrying one — two bodies and two counter-sinks from one slot. The exact yield per copy is queued for the checker rather than settled.
card_roles.Carrier Thrall: Fodder that pays twice: a 2/1 for two that dies into a 1/1 Eldrazi Scion which itself sacrifices for {C}. A body, then another body, then a mana.
card_roles.Butcher Ghoul: Undying makes it self-returning fodder — one free extra sacrifice per copy, with no card spent to get it back.
card_roles.Geralf's Messenger: Triple black for a 3/2 that drains an opponent for 2 on arrival and comes back once through undying. It enters tapped, so cast it for the body and the recursion, never for a block.
card_roles.Bloodghast: Returns from the graveyard on every land drop, which is roughly one free Yawgmoth activation a turn through the mid-game. It cannot block, which in a deck that wants its creatures dead is barely a drawback.
card_roles.Stitcher's Supplier: Mills three when it enters and three more when it dies, which is how Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Agadeem's Awakening get targets. It carries the deck's strongest synergy edges — score 3 to Agadeem's Awakening, Bloodghast, Persist and Victimize.
card_roles.Sedgemoor Witch: A 3/2 with menace and Ward 3 life that mints a Pest every time you cast an instant or sorcery — and this deck casts 20-plus of them. The ward is real protection in a list whose creatures are otherwise naked.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: A free sacrifice outlet that grants itself indestructible until end of turn, so it walks through your own sweepers and most of theirs. It grows whenever an opponent's creature dies, which your removal and your ignition both arrange.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: One mana, no tap, no cost — the cheapest free sacrifice outlet in the deck, and the one you want in an opening hand. It cannot block, and it grows a +1/+1 counter each time you feed it.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: A free outlet that scrys with every body, which is how a deck with five tutors still finds its half of the engine on turns nobody has a tutor.
card_roles.Woe Strider: A free outlet that arrives with its own Goat to eat, scrys on every activation, and escapes from the graveyard for {3}{B}{B} when the board is gone. Three jobs, three mana.
card_roles.Blasting Station: A free outlet that converts each body into a point of damage anywhere — and the only other card in the 99 that notices a token entering, since a creature entering untaps it.
card_roles.Spawning Pit: A free outlet that banks its bodies: two charge counters and {1} buy a 2/2 Spawn, so the fodder you spend comes back bigger than it left and with toughness enough to hold a counter.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: A free outlet that turns each body into {C}{C}, which is genuine acceleration in a deck making tokens for nothing. Engine mana is the deck's thinnest class — 53.0% drawn by turn 10 unassisted, 82.0% with a tutor.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: The same free outlet in coloured form: a body becomes one mana of any colour, which in mono-black means a body becomes a black mana you can spend on the proliferate or the tutor.
card_roles.Phyrexian Tower: A land that eats a creature for {B}{B} — a free outlet in a slot that costs you nothing, and the reason a hand light on artifacts can still convert.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: A Treasure for every other creature you control that dies, on a 1/4 body that survives three counters. Engine mana and a counter sink in the same card.
card_roles.Skullclamp: {1} to equip a 1/1 and draw two — a second, mana-priced draw engine for the turns Yawgmoth is not on the battlefield. Be precise about the mechanism: +1/-1 is a static modification and not a counter, so equipping never triggers the Nest.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Two cards and a Treasure at instant speed for a body you were going to spend anyway. This is what a spare token is worth when the board is stalled.
card_roles.Village Rites: One mana, one body, two cards, at instant speed — the cheapest way to convert a creature that is about to be exiled or countered into something permanent.
card_roles.Necropotence: The other draw engine, paid in the same currency as the first. Skip your draw step and buy cards a life at a time — and price it honestly against Yawgmoth's 1 life per activation, City of Brass, Ancient Tomb and Bitterblossom all charging the same account.
card_roles.Black Market Connections: Choose one or more every main phase: a Treasure, a card, or a 3/2 changeling body. All three modes are useful here and the third is fodder, so it rarely costs you a choice.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: A black source that turns surplus mana into cards once the hand is empty — which, in a deck drawing off every sacrifice, is a real state you reach.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Two mana, any card, no strings — the cleanest of the five tutors and the one that turns a stable board into the turn you go. Spend it once you know which half is missing, never on turn three.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Instant speed and 2 life for the exact card on top of your library. It costs you the draw, so cast it on the turn before you need the card, not the turn you do.
card_roles.Beseech the Mirror: Bargain is nearly free in a deck full of tokens and enchantments, and paying it lets you cast the fetched card outright if it costs 4 or less — which covers Nest of Scarabs, Blowfly Infestation and every drain in the list.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: A tutor whose additional cost is a creature, which is the one cost this deck never notices. Two mana and a spare Insect for any card in the library.
card_roles.Insatiable Avarice: Spree gives you two spells in one slot: {2} to put any card on top, or {B}{B} to draw three at the cost of 3 life. In a pinch it does both.
card_roles.Persist: Reanimation that doubles as ignition — stack 006 verified that a creature entering with a -1/-1 counter triggers the Nest via CR 122.6. Aim it at a body whose toughness survives the ride; a 1/1 returns as a 0/0 and leaves you only the Insect.
card_roles.Victimize: Sacrifice one creature, return two — a body converted into two bodies, which is exactly the exchange rate this engine wants after a sweeper.
card_roles.Animate Dead: Two mana for the best creature in any graveyard, yours or otherwise. It carries a synergy edge straight to Yawgmoth: the reanimated body is fodder the moment you need it.
card_roles.Agadeem's Awakening // Agadeem, the Unde: A mass reanimation that returns any number of creatures at different mana values, or a black source when the game has not gone that way yet. The modal land is why you can run it without diluting the base.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: One mana down, then {1}{B} and 2 life whenever you want a creature back in hand. Slow, permanent, and unanswerable by anything aimed at your graveyard once it is on the battlefield.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: A black source that channels away for a creature from the graveyard, and the cost drops {1} per legendary creature you control — there are six legendary permanents in the 99.
card_roles.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: Commander insurance for one mana and 2 life: the creature dies, your drain triggers, and it comes straight back. Or it is a tapped Swamp on the turn you need a land drop instead.
card_roles.Supernatural Stamina: The taxonomy has no role pattern for this one, which understates it — a one-mana instant that lets a creature die, pay out every death trigger you control, and return to the battlefield. Read it as commander insurance that also drains.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Haste and shroud for zero equip, which protects the hub the whole plan routes through. Know the cost of the shroud: while it is equipped you cannot target Yawgmoth with your own Malakir Rebirth or Supernatural Stamina.
card_roles.Deadly Rollick: Free exile for a creature while you control a commander — the answer to a hexproof threat or a combo body at instant speed. Exile leaves no corpse, so nothing of yours triggers off it.
card_roles.Snuff Out: Four life instead of four mana while you control a Swamp, which you always do. It destroys only nonblack creatures, so it is aimed outward at the table rather than at your own board.
card_roles.Fatal Push: One mana for anything at mana value 2, or mana value 4 once a permanent has left the battlefield under your control this turn — and something leaves under your control almost every turn.
card_roles.Dismember: -5/-5 for one mana and 4 life if you want it, which kills nearly anything at instant speed. It places no counters, so it triggers nothing of yours; treat it as pure interaction.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: The panic button, and it is a reset rather than a rebuild: -X/-X until end of turn places no counters at all, so Nest of Scarabs sees nothing. Your drains still fire on every death, which is why a Deluge with Bastion out is a table-wide burn spell.
card_roles.Ifnir Deadlands: A black source that becomes two -1/-1 counters on an opponent's creature by sacrificing a Desert — itself, or Survivors' Encampment. Sorcery speed, but it is ignition and removal from a land slot.
card_roles.Cabal Pit: A painful black source that, with seven cards in the graveyard, sacrifices itself to give something -2/-2. That is until end of turn and not counters, so it kills without feeding the Nest.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless on turn one or two, and the fastest route to a turn-two or turn-three Yawgmoth. It scores zero coloured sources in the audit — this is speed, not fixing.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana from a land at 2 damage a tap. A Game Changer, a genuine accelerant, and one more creditor on a life total this deck already spends freely.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two mana for a black source that never comes up dead. Unglamorous, and it is the difference between casting Yawgmoth on four and casting him on five.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: Three black from one, which puts Yawgmoth on the battlefield on turn two out of the right hand. The sim counts fast mana as drawn by turn 10 in 61.8% of games unassisted.
card_roles.Cabal Ritual: Three black for two, and five for two once seven cards are in your graveyard — a threshold this deck reaches on its own through Stitcher's Supplier and every creature it eats.
card_roles.Culling the Weak: One mana and a spare body for {B}{B}{B}{B}. The additional cost is the thing this deck manufactures for free, which makes it the most efficient ritual in the list.
card_roles.Command Tower: An untapped black source with no drawback whatsoever. In one colour that is all a fixing land needs to be.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: It makes whatever an opponent's lands make, and at a four-player table someone is on Swamps or a Command Tower. In practice, an untapped black source most games.
card_roles.City of Brass: An untapped source of any colour for 1 damage each tap. Cheap early, and worth pricing carefully once Necropotence and Yawgmoth are both drawing off the same life total.
card_roles.Gemstone Mine: Three taps of any colour before it sacrifices itself — enough for the early turns that matter and gone by the time you would miss it.
card_roles.Archway Commons: Enters tapped and asks {1} or it sacrifices itself. It is the softest land in the base, and the tempo cost lands squarely on turns one through three.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: A tapped black source that scrys when its mana casts a creature sharing a type with Yawgmoth — Human or Cleric, which several bodies in the list are.
card_roles.Survivors' Encampment: Tap an untapped creature for any colour, which turns a spare Insect into a mana. It is also a Desert, which is what Ifnir Deadlands wants to eat.
card_roles.Bojuka Bog: A tapped black source that exiles a graveyard on arrival — the only graveyard answer anywhere in the 99, so hold it for the reanimator seat rather than dropping it on turn two.
card_roles.Swamp: Twenty-two of them, and 35 of the deck's 36 lands make black. The base is boring on purpose; the interesting decisions all happen after the mana is spent.

mulligan:
The keep test is not "do I have the combo". It is: can this hand make bodies, and can it kill one of them for free? Fodder and a free outlet are the two classes every line in the deck routes through, and they are also the two the sim finds earliest — mean turn 2.671 and 2.682 respectively.

You can afford to be selective and you rarely have to be. The goldfish keeps its first seven 81.9% of the time at a mean of 0.21 mulligans, and 3,791 of its kept hands hold exactly three lands. Two to five lands is the keep band. Below two you are hoping; above five you are drawing air, because 51 of 64 spells cost three or less and mean available mana is 3.927 on turn four.

Keep on sight: two to four lands plus a renewable body — Bitterblossom, Ophiomancer, Carrier Thrall, Bloodghast, Butcher Ghoul, Stitcher's Supplier. Bitterblossom on turn two is the best two-drop in the deck; it makes a Faerie every upkeep for 1 life and rebuilds through a sweeper on its own. Keep any hand with Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb, Dark Ritual, Culling the Weak or Cabal Ritual and a black source — fast mana is drawn by turn 10 in 61.8% of games unassisted, so a hand that already has it is ahead of the curve you were dealt.

Keep a tutor with almost anything castable. A tutor cannot fetch itself, which is why the "tutor drawn" row is 61.7% in both columns and why it is the real ceiling on the whole finish. Do not spend it on turn three, though — it is the card you cash once the board is stable and you know exactly which half is missing.

Ship these without ceremony. Payoffs with no bodies: Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar are all blanks until something is dying. Ship hands built on Mikaeus, the Unhallowed alone — {3}{B}{B}{B} against 3.927 mana on turn four is a turn-seven card, and the eight two-card infinites he headlines are unverified. And ship the Blowfly Infestation plus Nest of Scarabs hand that has nothing else: stack 001 proved that pair is drainless on a bare board and needs your drain plus two spare bodies before it is worth anything.

One-landers go back even holding a rock. This deck has 36 lands and no way to find one.
upgrades:
Ten names render below, and the arithmetic that ranks them is the same arithmetic that runs the deck. Every verified engine here ends by body exhaustion — stack 005's final state says it outright, "no creature other than Yawgmoth left to sacrifice - not life, not library" — so a card that renews a body is worth more than a card that adds a payoff. That is the first of the two holes the list answers.

The second is a kill that does not route through Nest of Scarabs. The hub is a singleton with no redundancy in the 99, it is an enchantment, and this deck holds no enchantment removal to trade back with. A finish that closes on a different axis is worth real slots: Exquisite Blood pairs with South Wind Avatar, which is already sleeved, and Reassembling Skeleton turns "{1}{B}: Return this card from your graveyard to the battlefield tapped" into a Yawgmoth activation every single turn.

Watch what the numbers refuse to move. Bracket 4 before, bracket 4 after, on all ten entries — these extend engines, they do not escalate the power level. And every combo line any entry opens carries the same stamp, needs a stack scenario, because the checker has already overturned three Commander Spellbook claims about this exact list: stacks 001, 004 and 005.

Two entries are pure mana rather than pure engine, and they are underrated here. Cabal Coffers reads {2} and a tap for black equal to your Swamps, and 22 of this deck's lands are Swamps — the largest single mana gain available, on a land, costing no spell slot. Grave Pact and Dictate of Erebos fill an effect class the 99 holds none of: a deck that sacrifices a creature nearly every turn converts each activation into an edict aimed at all three opponents.

One caution on the machinery underneath. The obsolescence index flags 13 cards in this 99 as having newer, textually similar analogues, and it scores text similarity plus generic advantages — lower mana value, better toughness, an extra keyword. It does not price the thing this deck actually buys, which is a sacrifice outlet that costs no mana. Read those flags as leads, not as verdicts.
mana_base:
Start where mono-colour makes the audit easy, then look at the one place it does not. Black carries 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources — 70.0 pips across 53 cards, up to triple-black in a single cost, first demanded on turn one. Pip share and source share cannot disagree in a deck with one colour, so the interesting question is never which colour, it is how many.

Thirty-six land copies across 15 entries, 22 of them Swamp. Thirty-five of those 36 make black. The yardstick asks for 36 sources and the audit's note is blunt about what that means: in a 36-land deck the target is a yardstick, not a possibility. Lands alone put black on curve at 89.5% — half a point under 90%, and the half point is arithmetic, not a build error.

Ten nonland producers close it. Four rocks, six rituals and two dorks lift the count to 45 sources and on-curve black to 97.0%. Mind which ones score zero: Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb and Ashnod's Altar produce nothing coloured under the audit's unconditional-mana rule, so they buy speed rather than fixing. Restricted mana: none anywhere in the 99.

Four lands enter tapped — Archway Commons, Bojuka Bog, Castle Locthwain and Path of Ancestry — which is the whole tempo cost of the base. The rest is paid in life. City of Brass, Ancient Tomb, Cabal Pit and Ifnir Deadlands all charge you, and they queue behind Necropotence, Black Market Connections, Bitterblossom, Vampiric Tutor and 1 life per Yawgmoth activation.

The development curve is what a 36-land deck looks like when it stops needing lands. Land-drop hit rate runs 92.4% on turn three, 58.7% on turn six and 39.9% on turn ten, while mean available mana climbs 3.927, 5.241, 7.109. Nothing in the deck costs five, and only three cards cost more than four — so from turn six onward the surplus is not for casting spells. It is for the tutor, and for Yawgmoth's "{B}{B}, Discard a card: Proliferate," which stacks 002 and 003 price at exactly one extra drain.
threat_assessment:
The table starts its clock on you the moment Yawgmoth resolves, and the goldfish says that moment is turn four. Mean cast turn 4.287, exactly turn four in 7,208 of 10,000 games, on the battlefield in 98.6% of them and down by turn six in 91.3%. Nothing else this deck does is that reliable. Plan the whole game around the fact that your best card is also your first tell.

Know what three opponents read off it. The bracket report puts you at floor 4, driven by four Game Changers — Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Necropotence, Vampiric Tutor — and eight two-card infinites. Add five tutors and, from across the table, you look like a combo deck. strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection warns that "combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player" — read that in reverse and it is a description of you.

Now hold the number that makes all of this manageable. A fully assembled engine — Yawgmoth, Nest of Scarabs, an each-opponent drain — is seven drains. Stack 002 proves it with Bastion of Remembrance, stack 003 proves it with Zulaport Cutthroat, both checker-pass, both landing on the same figure: seven life from each opponent, 28 across a four-opponent table. The pod goes from 40 to 33.

So you telegraph lethality you do not yet have. That is my read, and it is this deck's central political problem: your scary board is a clock, and the table prices it as a kill. The good news is that it is a sequencing problem, and sequencing problems are the ones you get to solve for free.

The read hierarchy is specific. Bitterblossom, Ophiomancer, Carrier Thrall, Bloodghast and Sedgemoor Witch are furniture — they read as a fair sacrifice deck and they eat almost no removal. Yawgmoth himself reads as a draw engine and a lightning rod; expect to pay for him and price the recast in before you cast him. Nest of Scarabs is the card that changes the room, because it is the hub every verified line routes through and nothing in the 99 rebuys an enchantment.

Two board states genuinely flip you to archenemy, and both reads are correct. Blowfly Infestation beside Nest of Scarabs with a drain and two spare bodies is the real thing — stack 001 proves that loop unbounded and puts four opponents from 40 to 0 in 38 completed iterations. Mikaeus, the Unhallowed is the shared half of seven of the eight two-card infinites on the bracket report. Present either one next to a drain only on a turn you can act.

The rule that follows: lead fodder, hold the hub. Cast Nest of Scarabs on the turn it converts, not the turn you can first afford it. strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window tells you to "sequence the scariest piece last so the deflection budget lasts until the turn you take it" — with a three-card assembly, the last piece is the one everybody would have answered.

Tutors are information, so spend them at the right speed. Vampiric Tutor is an instant: fire it on the end step before your untap and the table sees a card leave your hand, not a plan (strategy:tempo.sequencing prefers "committing at the end step before your own turn"). Demonic Tutor, Diabolic Intent and Beseech the Mirror are sorceries and announce the go turn simply by being cast. The payoff is enormous — either kill assembles by turn ten in 4.6% of games on natural draws and 31.4% once a tutor fetches the missing half — so protect the tempo of that spend as carefully as you choose the target.

The go decision is body arithmetic, done before the first activation rather than during it. Every engine stack that ran to exhaustion ended the same way; stack 005 names it "by body exhaustion." Count spare bodies, then count survivable toughness on top: South Wind Avatar's four toughness is worth exactly +4 activations (stack 005), and Yawgmoth's "{B}{B}, Discard a card: Proliferate" is worth exactly one more drain — 8 and 32 instead of 7 and 28 (stack 002).

Subtract one thing from that count. Ophiomancer makes its Snake only "if you control no Snakes," and South Wind Avatar is a Snake Spirit Avatar. While the Avatar is on the battlefield, your per-upkeep deathtouch body stops arriving. The Avatar is still worth every mana — just do the arithmetic with it, not around it.

Life is your other currency and you spend it constantly: a point per Yawgmoth activation, plus Necropotence, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, City of Brass, Ancient Tomb, Cabal Pit and Ifnir Deadlands. strategy:life-as-resource is on your side early — "early points are cheap and late points are priceless" — and the engine pays you back. Stacks 002 and 003 both end with you at 42, above where the turn started.

The payment makes you archenemy in exactly one shape: a visibly low total, no drain on the battlefield, and an untapped combat board across from you. Do not Necropotence into that picture. Track each seat's clock on you separately and stop spending one turn early rather than one turn late.

Then embrace being the threat, because the pivot is smaller than it feels. It is not "can I kill the pod," it is "can I kill one seat" — go when the lowest life total at the table is at or under your spare bodies plus the counters your surviving toughness can absorb. And this engine leaves you rebuilt when it stalls: stack 002 ends with five fresh cards in hand, stack 005 with eight. strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window asks you to "prefer win attempts that leave a rebuilt position if they fail." Yours always does. Take the window.

One last piece of free armour the table forgets: protection from Humans. A Human source cannot target Yawgmoth (CR 702.16b), Human damage to him is prevented (CR 702.16e), and Human creatures cannot block him when he attacks (CR 702.16f) — real text in a format thick with Human commanders. Lightning Greaves is the other insurance, and equip activates only as a sorcery (CR 702.6a), so you buy it the turn before the removal, never in response to it (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance).
matchups:
Sweeper control is your best matchup and you should be visibly delighted about it. With an each-opponent drain on the battlefield, a wrath is a drain per body, and the goldfish has 6.625 bodies on your side of the table by turn ten. Five recursion slots and self-returning bodies — Bloodghast's landfall, Butcher Ghoul's undying, Retched Wretch — mean the rebuild is already bought. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math tells you to "buy resilience instead of restraint," and this list did exactly that, so deploy the fodder freely.

Two things in that matchup actually cost you. Removal on Yawgmoth costs a tempo turn and the recast tax; pay it and move on. Enchantment removal on Nest of Scarabs is the real one, because nothing in the 99 rebuys an enchantment — that is the single board state where your tutor is a rebuild rather than a finish, and you should spend it that way without flinching.

Two of your own cards flip that matchup. Toxic Deluge is a sweeper you get to profit from, since with a drain out every body it kills pays you — but be precise about it, because -X/-X is not counters and Nest of Scarabs does not trigger off it. Massacre Girl, Known Killer is the opposite: "Creatures you control have wither," so your combat damage to creatures arrives as -1/-1 counters, and that does trigger the Nest.

Stax and tax splits down the middle, and you must know which half you are in. Yawgmoth's ability costs no mana, so Sphere effects, Winter Orb and Rule of Law do not touch the engine once it is online — they tax getting the hub down and casting the tutor, which is a different problem. What beats you is class coverage: no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell, and one graveyard answer in Bojuka Bog. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite is blunt about the cost — "breadth before depth" — and mono-black covers one class.

Name your outs out loud so you do not freeze. Cursed Totem reads "Activated abilities of creatures can't be activated," which switches off Yawgmoth, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Woe Strider and Yahenni all at once — your outlets under it are Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Blasting Station, Spawning Pit and Phyrexian Tower, none of which are creatures. Pithing Needle naming Yawgmoth has the same shape and the same outs. Blowfly Infestation plus Nest of Scarabs is triggered rather than activated, so it runs under both.

The role flips against a lock. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial: "you rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown, racing the lock's completion." Spend the tutor early rather than optimally, and answer the compounding second piece rather than the first inconvenience.

Graveyard hate earns its own paragraph, because the class hits you harder than its reputation suggests. Rest in Peace exiles cards and tokens instead of putting them into a graveyard, and "dies" means "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" (CR 700.4) — so under it Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar stop draining altogether, not merely stop recurring. Mirkwood Bats is the exception worth memorising: it keys on "whenever you create or sacrifice a token," not on deaths, so it is the one drain still live. Grafdigger's Cage is narrower and stops creature cards in graveyards from entering, which blanks undying, Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Bloodghast while leaving tokens untouched.

That gives you a clean tutoring rule against a graveyard-hate seat: point at Blowfly Infestation and Nest of Scarabs, never at Mikaeus. The Mikaeus kill assembles by turn ten in 24.8% of games with tutor help and is entirely graveyard-dependent; the Blowfly half is 32.1% and does not care about the yard at all.

Aggro is favoured, and the reason is arithmetic rather than answers. strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry: "aggro's math is worst hit — ~120 combined life behind three defenses makes incremental combat damage a losing plan." Against you it is worse, because chump blocking is free: a death is a card off Yawgmoth and, with a drain out, damage to the whole table. Ophiomancer's Snake, South Wind Avatar and Grave Titan all block with deathtouch — and note before you plan a turn on paper that Bloodghast and Carrion Feeder cannot block at all.

Let their creatures live where you can. An opponent's 2/2 "does not bound the engine, it EXTENDS it by two activations" (stack 002), so a table with no creatures is genuinely the worst board this engine can face. Your -1/-1 package doubles as interaction — deck-facts counts 10 debuff effects, 3 spot removal and 3 sweepers — which is how a list with seven or eight dedicated answers survives early pressure. Before you accept a race, count what the engine has already spent from your total.

Combo is your worst matchup and the frame should say so plainly. Your cheap interaction is Deadly Rollick, Snuff Out, Fatal Push and Dismember; every one targets a creature, and Snuff Out only hits nonblack ones. Against a noncreature kill you hold nothing, and there are no counterspells to find.

So change how you spend. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy names the countervailing rule — "held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now" — which means you do not save Snuff Out for a better target. Then race, because racing is a real plan here: commander down by turn six in 91.3%, a drain in hand by turn ten in 85.4% with tutor help, and a kill assembled in 31.4%.

Blood Artist is the card that changes shape in this matchup. On the same board that pays Bastion and Zulaport 28 life, it pays 8 — stack 004's verdict is "NOT A KILL, AND NOT EVEN CLOSE" — so it is removal-adjacent reach rather than a payoff you assemble toward. Its one virtue is that "target player loses 1 life" concentrates: all eight at one seat, 40 to 32. Aimed at the combo player who is one turn from going off, that is a line, not a consolation. Spend your deflection budget on that seat and take your own window while three players' interaction is pointed at them (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection).
